A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NGS-based QSR approach is highly promising for the deconvolution of the composition of viral quasispeces, especially in the context of HCV/HIV coinfection.

the prevalence of Gt overlapping infection and minor RAVs is higher in coinfected hemophilia patients and patients who had received transfusions, and the prevalence of Gts and RAVs in minor haplotypes is higher than in dominant haplotypes.
the Q80K variant is a potential marker for HCV/HIV-coinfection in hemophiliacs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, for HCV/HIV-coinfected hemophiliac patients, the risk of treatment failure due to RAVs may be increased by Gt1a and Gt1b infection, particularly when the latter is associated with the Q80K mutation, whereas for HCV monoinfection, the risk may be increased by the Gt1b and Gt1a infections, particularly the latter when it is associated with the RAV Q80R.

the prevalence of Gt 1b-Q80R and Q80K in HCV monoinfection and coinfected patients is associated with the history of blood transfusions and hemophilia, respectively, and that the prevalence of Q80K is particularly high in HCV/HCV coinfected hemophilia patients.
the QSR-based genetic analysis of pre-existing RAVs and their interrelationships is a promising approach for understanding viral quasispecies dynamics and predicting the outcome of DAA treatment.
